A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MECAT benchmark and DATE metric. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on MECAT-Caption and MECAT-QA, metric comparisons, embedding analyses and LLM-as-judge reliability results.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds broader model comparisons, human annotation audits, weighting sensitivity, bootstrap analyses and hallucination case studies.

M1.justification: The expert-model, DeepSeek-R1 reasoning and filtering pipeline is retained, as is DATE's combination of weighted semantic similarity and cross-sample discriminability. Appendix E specifies previously unspecified embedding-level TF-IDF calculations; the PDFs do not establish an underlying procedural replacement.

E1.justification: Both versions use approximately 20,000 ACAV100M clips across the same eight domains, with the same captioning and QA tasks. The external datasets in the embedding comparison are retained. New human audits and silence case studies examine existing MECAT coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2 and 3 expand from 6 captioning and 4 QA models to 17 and 15. Audio Flamingo 3 replaces Audio Flamingo 2 in these evaluations, while additions include Phi-4-Multimodal, Baichuan models, MiMo-Audio, Step-Audio-2-mini, Qwen3 variants and Gemini models. Audio Flamingo 2 remains part of benchmark construction.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces a 150-pair human preference protocol and a 700-sample audit involving 20 audio professionals and a five-level relevance scale. It also tests alternative caption aggregation weights and varying bootstrap sample sizes; Appendices J and K report separate similarity and discriminability measurements. These are added evaluation designs, not established reruns under changed settings for the original comparisons.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct annotation-quality validation, sensitivity to aggregation weights, DATE stability across sample sizes and alignment with human preferences in Appendix F. Appendix J examines similarity versus discriminability, and Appendix L adds two silent-segment hallucination cases. These substantially extend v1's metric examples, distribution plots and judge-reliability analysis.

E5.justification: The existing Fleiss' kappa results are retained, but v3 adds Wilson confidence intervals, Wilcoxon tests with Bonferroni correction, a Mann-Whitney comparison and effect sizes. Its bootstrap study reports 50 iterations per group and sampling ratio, confidence intervals, coefficients of variation and maximum deviations. These are new statistical procedures, not evidence of increased model-generation runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive model and validation results, including Gemini-3-Pro's 53.1 caption score and Qwen3-Omni's 52.3 QA score. Retained models also have revised Table 2 aggregates despite unchanged component entries: Pengi changes from 30.6 to 29.4 and Qwen2.5-Omni 7B from 43.0 to 42.6. These are numerical revisions rather than demonstrated performance changes; corresponding retained QA scores remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix E adds formal definitions for semantic term frequency using squared embedding similarities and embedding-aware document frequency and IDF. v1 gives only generic TF-IDF factors. This is a limited mathematical specification of DATE's weighting component; the principal similarity, rank and harmonic-mean equations remain equivalent, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain a multi-expert, reasoning-assisted benchmark for fine-grained captioning and QA, and DATE for rewarding detailed, discriminative descriptions. The abstract and introduction retain this scientific scope; expanded validation and model comparisons support these contributions rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: Section 6.4 adds specific limitations concerning short clips, residual annotation errors, entity swaps and reduced DATE discrimination on homogeneous corpora. New discussions interpret expert-error independence, weighting stability, discriminability and hallucination behavior. These substantially extend v1's brief limitations and model-specialization discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds computational details for embedding normalization, token exclusions, TF/DF accumulation and weighting. Appendix I extends prompt assignments to the added models and clarifies default versus overridden system prompts. The construction-model inventory, synthesis prompts and code/data access statement are substantially retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for newer evaluated models, WavCaps and MMAR, and replaces the unrelated defect-prediction FENSE reference with an audio-caption evaluation reference. The main positioning against coarse annotations, closed-ended QA and insufficiently discriminative metrics remains intact.

P1.justification: Much of the abstract, method description and prompt appendices is preserved. Editorial changes include expanded introductory motivation, numbered subsections, rewritten performance discussion, a shortened conclusion, consolidated references and new disclosure text. These are localized structural and language revisions around the expanded scientific content.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the overview figure, regroups the expert diagram and merges v1's Figures 5 and 6 into a recolored, multipanel Figure 5. The model tables expand substantially, Table 3 changes orientation, and numerous validation and analysis tables appear in the appendices. The document also adopts a different conference layout.

improvement.justification: The human preference study and 700-sample expert audit address an important weakness in v1: the lack of direct human evidence for automatically generated caption quality. Statistical uncertainty, sensitivity analyses and explicit applicability limits substantially strengthen the paper's evidential foundation. Numerical inconsistencies remain, including Qwen3-Omni's pure-speech similarity of 41.0 in Table J.1 versus 34.1 in Table K.1, but these do not outweigh the substantial validation gains.
